extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for enforcing, protecting and managing IP in South Africa, including bioprospecting/ABS permit requirements, ownership of IP from publicly financed R&D, available funding/support programmes, and procedural steps for IPR enforcement and civil proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: BABS (Access and Benefit Sharing Regulations) — scope and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Governs the discovery and commercialisation phases of bioprospecting projects, and set out the form and content of, and requirements and criteria for benefit-sharing and material transfer agreements and the administration process of the Bioprospecting Trust Fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BABS when planning commercial bioprospecting; consult DEA guidelines and the BABS Regulations (including Appendix 3 templates) for the required form and content of benefit-sharing and material transfer agreements and for administration of the Bioprospecting Trust Fund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permits for bioprospecting (BABS / NEMBA) — who needs a permit
rubrics_metrics.description: A permit is required for anyone carrying out bioprospecting involving indigenous biological resources (and, if applicable, associated traditional use or knowledge), and for anyone exporting indigenous biological resources for the purposes of bioprospecting or other research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A permit will only be issued where: material disclosure to stakeholders has been made; prior informed consent to the bioprospecting has been obtained; and the Minister is satisfied that statutory conditions are met. Stakeholders include those who gave access (e.g., land owners) and indigenous communities whose traditional knowledge contributed to the bioprospecting. Benefit-sharing agreements and material transfer agreements must be entered into with relevant stakeholders. The DEA guide assists with completing permit applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit issuance conditions — material disclosure and prior informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A permit will only be issued if there is material disclosure to stakeholders, if their prior informed consent to the bioprospecting has been obtained, and if the Minister is satisfied that certain conditions, as set out in the legislation, have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure full material disclosure and documented prior informed consent from both land owners and indigenous communities where applicable; include benefit-sharing terms and material transfer agreement terms as required by BABS. Use the DEA guidance and BABS templates to prepare compliant applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR-PFRD Act — ownership of IP from publicly financed R&D
rubrics_metrics.description: IP emanating from publicly financed research and development is owned by the recipient of the funding (e.g., higher education institutions, science councils, other institutions identified by the Minister).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act provides three possible ownership options: the default position (owned by the recipient that undertakes R&D using funding from a funding agency); co-ownership (where a private entity can co-own if there was a contribution of resources, joint IP creation, appropriate benefit-sharing arrangements, and a commercialisation agreement); and a full cost arrangement where IP ownership may be negotiated. Recipients should check funder terms and institutional policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIPMO obligations and expectations for recipients of public R&D funding
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Intellectual Property Management Office (NIPMO) is responsible for implementing the IPR-PFRD Act and aims to ensure recipients assess, record and report on the benefit to society of IP from publicly financed R&D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must protect IP from appropriation, ensure it is available to the people of South Africa, and identify commercialisation opportunities. Maintain records and reporting consistent with NIPMO requirements and institutional policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available support and funding programmes for innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Various national and international programmes support inventors, SMEs and institutions with funding, incubation and patent assistance (examples: WIPO IAP, Technology Innovation Agency (TIA), SPII, THRIP, Seed Fund, SEDA Technology Programme, Innovation Hub).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate programme depending on stage of technology readiness, funding required and commercialisation goals. Examples: WIPO IAP matches inventors with volunteer patent attorneys; TIA funding is differentiated by TRL and purpose; SPII funds technology and market validation; THRIP funds applied research; Seed Fund assists SMMEs and HEIs with commercialisation bridging finance; SEDA/STP supports incubation, market validation and small-scale manufacturing; Innovation Hub offers incubation in specified sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary steps before litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before instituting formal court proceedings, consider preliminary steps and alternative measures (these may provide relief or protect the business without going to court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key preliminary steps include: IPR searches to identify infringement and existing rights; proprietor searches; internet and company/director searches to obtain details of alleged infringers; sending a letter of demand to seek compliance or negotiation; and obtaining an opinion on merits from an IPR specialist or advocate to assess likely defences and merits before proceeding to court. Validity searches are recommended to be conducted by a specialised attorney or agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR searches — purpose and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR searches are used to identify infringement problems and provide background and details of any existing rights of an alleged wrongdoer, and possible defences that may be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct proprietor searches to obtain details of IPRs in the name of the same proprietor; searches provide details of IPRs recorded on the patents, designs, and trade marks registers. Due to technical nature and grounds for dispute, validity searches are recommended to be conducted by a specialised attorney or agent. Online searches can be done via CIPC IPOnline; company and director information via BizPortal/CIPC Entity Search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter of demand — use and cost-saving tip
rubrics_metrics.description: A written document informing an alleged wrongdoer of the legal claim, setting out the desired relief and providing notice of intention to bring proceedings if demands are not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sending a letter of demand can save costs: if a summons is issued without a letter of demand and the wrongdoer then complies, you may be liable for the costs of preparing and issuing the summons. In some cases (e.g., copyright) a letter may be necessary to complete a cause of action; consider issuing one to preserve cost recovery and encourage resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim proceedings (interim interdicts) — criteria for urgent relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim interdicts (preliminary injunctions) are available for urgent relief and are instituted by way of an application supported by evidence confirming certain factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant must demonstrate: the subsistence of a clear right in the relevant IPR that is valid and in force; likelihood of irreparable harm if interim relief is not granted; that the balance of convenience favours granting the interim relief; and that there is no other satisfactory remedy. Evidence should support these elements to persuade the wrongdoer to comply or to obtain urgent court relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anton Piller orders — preservation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Court orders allowing the complainant to search and seize evidence from the wrongdoer’s premises without prior notice to prevent removal or destruction of relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts impose strict compliance and procedural requirements before granting an Anton Piller order; a supervising attorney is appointed to ensure compliance with the scope of the order. Requests for discovery of documents can only be called for when proceedings are instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal costs and disbursements in IP litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation to protect and enforce IPRs can be costly; courts have discretion to award costs in favour of the substantially successful party, and costs are based on tariffs in the court rules or negotiated fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disbursements include court fees, counsel fees and expert witnesses. Common cost awards are party-and-party costs (based on court tariffs). Courts may award attorney-and-client costs (which may exceed tariffs) or attorney-and-own-client costs in exceptional cases, and rarely punitive costs. Negotiated fees usually apply to IPR litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal IPR civil proceedings — application vs action
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings may be commenced by either application (motion) or action (trial) depending on whether facts are in dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application proceedings: used where there is no dispute of fact; evidence contained in affidavits and ordinarily no oral evidence is heard (oral evidence if disputes arise). Action proceedings: used where a dispute of fact exists or is likely; commenced by issuing summons and particulars of claim; evidence by expert witnesses is given orally, with examination and cross-examination; affidavits may supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging validity of IPR — opposition and cancellation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms exist to challenge the validity or registration of an IPR and to stop unauthorised use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For trade marks: once accepted the application is advertised and any interested party may, within three months from the date of advertisement, oppose the application (opposition term can be extended via online application; further extensions require consent or good cause). Grounds for opposition are set out in Section 10 of the Trade Marks Act. Proceedings can be lodged before the Registrar of Trade Marks and transferred to the High Court. Cancellation (revocation) proceedings can attack registration on various grounds, possibly resulting in cancellation, partial cancellation, or limitation of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging unauthorised use / infringement — remedies available
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant IPR legislation sets out the circumstances of infringement, defences and remedies; relief available from courts includes several possible orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available reliefs include: an interdict; delivery up of infringing products or removal of the infringing IPR; an enquiry into damages suffered; payment of a reasonable royalty in lieu of damages; costs; and any further or alternative relief deemed appropriate by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing venues and institutional powers for IP disputes in South Africa
rubrics_metrics.description: IP-related disputes are generally heard in the High Court; there is the Court of the Commissioner of Patents and registrars with specific powers under the Patents Act, Design Act and Trade Marks Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South Africa does not have specialised IP courts other than the Court of the Commissioner of Patents. Formal IP disputes are heard in the High Court as court of first instance, but particular matters may be heard in several courts or tribunals. Registrars have powers and duties under the respective Acts and regulations.
